questions.q: The criteria table on this page compares the ideal properties of a drug for which two processes?
questions.exp: The table is headed with two columns, 'Absorption' and 'Excretion', and lists the solubility, ionization, pH relation and polarity required for each. (Book p5)

questions.q: As per the criteria table, a drug should be lipid soluble for absorption and ________ for excretion.
questions.exp: Solubility row: absorption requires lipid solubility, excretion requires water solubility — the basis of the WIPE mnemonic. (Book p5)

questions.q: For absorption to occur, the drug must be present in which form?
questions.exp: Ionization row: absorption needs the unionised form; the ionised form is required for excretion. (Book p5)

questions.q: For excretion of a drug into urine, the drug must be:
questions.exp: The excretion column requires the ionised, polar, water-soluble form — an ionised drug is not reabsorbed and is excreted. (Book p5)

questions.q: The table states that for absorption, the relation of the pH of the medium to the pH of the drug is:
questions.exp: Row 'Relation of pH of medium': absorption 'Equal', excretion 'Unequal' — for absorption the pH of the medium equals the pH of the drug (its pKa). (Book p5)

questions.q: For excretion, the relation of the pH of the drug to the pH of the medium is:
questions.exp: The excretion column reads 'Unequal' — the pH of the drug and the pH of the medium are different, so the drug stays ionised in urine and is excreted. (Book p5)

questions.q: As per the criteria table, the polarity required for absorption is:
questions.exp: Absorption requires a non-polar molecule (lipid soluble); excretion requires a polar (water-soluble) molecule. (Book p5)

questions.q: The mnemonic 'LUNJA' stands for the properties favouring:
questions.exp: LUNJA is written under the absorption column: Lipid soluble, Unionised, Non polar, pH equal to that of the drug/medium, Absorption. (Book p5)

questions.q: The mnemonic 'WIPE' describes the properties favouring:
questions.exp: WIPE is written under the excretion column — Water soluble, Ionised, pH of drug and medium unequal/different, Polar. (Book p5)

questions.q: In the mnemonic WIPE, the letter 'W' stands for:
questions.exp: WIPE = Water soluble, Ionised, pH unequal (different), Polar — the profile that ensures the drug is excreted. (Book p5)

questions.q: An acidic drug is unionized in an:
opts: Acidic medium such as the stomach
Basic medium such as the small intestine
questions.exp: 'Acidic drug – Acidic medium: Stomach' — an acidic drug stays unionised in the acidic gastric medium. (Book p5)

questions.q: A basic drug is unionized in a:
opts: Basic medium such as the small intestine
Acidic medium such as the stomach
questions.exp: 'Basic drug – Basic medium: Small Intestine' — the basic drug remains unionised in the alkaline medium of the small intestine. (Book p5)

questions.q: The example given for an acidic drug that is unionized in the stomach is:
questions.exp: 'Eg: Aspirin (Acidic drug) is unionized in stomach' — aspirin is the cited acidic drug of unionization. (Book p5)

questions.q: Although aspirin is unionized in the stomach, its maximum absorption occurs in the:
questions.exp: Maximum absorption of the unionized drug (both acidic and basic drugs) happens in the small intestine, chiefly the duodenum. (Book p5)

questions.q: The reason maximum absorption of unionized drug occurs in the small intestine rather than the stomach is the:
opts: High lipid content of the medium
questions.exp: The text attributes it to the duodenum's large surface area, which outweighs the stomach's favourable acidity. (Book p5)

questions.q: Which statement about absorption of unionized drug is correct as per the text?
opts: Only acidic unionized drugs are absorbed in the small intestine
Only basic unionized drugs are absorbed in the small intestine
Both acidic and basic unionized drugs are maximally absorbed in the small intestine
Acidic drugs are maximally absorbed in the stomach
questions.exp: 'But max absorption of unionized drug (Both Acidic & Basic) happens in Small intestine: Duodenum (D/t large surface area)'. (Book p5)

questions.q: In short bowel syndrome, resection of the small intestine leads to:
questions.exp: 'Resection of small intestine → ↓ Absorption of drug' — loss of absorptive surface reduces drug absorption. (Book p5)

questions.q: The management of drug therapy in short bowel syndrome is to:
opts: Increase the dosage of drug or change the route
questions.exp: 'mx: ↑ Dosage of drug or change route' — since absorption is reduced, dose is increased or the route is changed (e.g., parenteral). (Book p5)

questions.q: A patient with short bowel syndrome on an oral drug fails to respond. The dose-independent explanation is:
opts: Loss of small intestinal surface area reduces absorption
Renal tubular secretion of the drug
questions.exp: Resection of the small intestine decreases drug absorption in short bowel syndrome; the book's management is to increase dosage or change the route. (Book p5)

questions.q: Ionization for the purpose of excretion occurs when the pH of the drug and the pH of the medium are:
questions.exp: 'IONIZATION (EXCRETION): pH of drug and pH of medium are different' — an un-ionisable match is required for absorption, a difference for excretion. (Book p5)

questions.q: In acidic drug toxicity, urine is made:
questions.exp: 'Acidic drug toxicity → make urine Basic' — alkalinising urine ionizes the acidic drug and traps it for excretion. (Book p5)

questions.q: Which of the following are cited as examples of acidic drugs causing toxicity?
questions.exp: Under 'Acidic drug toxicity' the text lists aspirin, phenobarbital and methotrexate as the acidic drugs treated by alkalinising the urine. (Book p5)

questions.q: The urine alkalinizer used in acidic drug toxicity is:
questions.exp: 'By bicarbonate: urine Alkalinizer' — sodium bicarbonate is used to alkalinise urine in aspirin/phenobarbital/methotrexate toxicity. (Book p5)

questions.q: In basic drug toxicity, the urine is made:
questions.exp: 'Basic drug toxicity → make urine Acidic' — acidifying urine ionizes the basic drug, trapping it in the tubular fluid for excretion. (Book p5)

questions.q: The basic drug listed as an example of drug toxicity treated by acidifying urine is:
questions.exp: Amphetamine is the example under basic drug toxicity; aspirin, phenobarbital and methotrexate are the acidic drugs. (Book p5)

questions.q: The urine acidifier used in basic drug toxicity is:
questions.exp: 'By Ammonium chloride: urine Acidifier' — ammonium chloride acidifies urine to excrete basic drugs such as amphetamine. (Book p5)

questions.q: Which two agents are listed as other examples of urine acidifiers?
questions.exp: 'Note: Other examples for urine acidifiers are Vit C, Cranberry juice.' (Book p5)

questions.q: A patient presents with salicylate (acidic drug) overdose. The most appropriate urinary measure is:
opts: Acidify the urine with ammonium chloride
Give vitamin C to acidify urine
questions.exp: Aspirin is an acidic drug; the text advises making the urine basic with bicarbonate so the ionised drug is trapped and excreted. (Book p5)

questions.q: The rationale for alkalinising urine in acidic drug toxicity is that the drug becomes:
questions.exp: In an alkaline urine an acidic drug is ionised; an ionised, polar drug is excreted rather than reabsorbed — the ionization criterion for excretion. (Book p5)

questions.q: In amphetamine poisoning, acidifying the urine works because in an acidic medium a basic drug is:
questions.exp: A basic drug placed in acidic urine becomes ionised (pH of drug and medium differ), so it is trapped and excreted — the basis of giving ammonium chloride. (Book p5)

questions.q: For an acidic drug, the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation as given is:
questions.exp: 'Acidic drug → log [Unionized]/[Ionized] = pKa − pH (of medium)'. (Book p6)

questions.q: For a basic drug, the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation as given is:
questions.exp: 'Basic drug → log [Ionized]/[Unionized] = pKa − pH' — note the ratio is inverted compared with an acidic drug. (Book p6)

questions.q: In the two equations, which component is measured 'of medium'?
questions.exp: The equations are written as pKa − pH, with the parenthetical note '(of medium)' attached to pH — pKa belongs to the drug, pH to the medium. (Book p6)

questions.q: pKa is defined in the text as the pH of the medium at which:
opts: 50% drug is ionized and 50% is unionized
The drug is maximally lipid soluble
questions.exp: 'pKa: pH of the medium at which 50% drug is ionized & 50 is unionized'. (Book p6)

questions.q: For an acidic drug with pKa 4 in the stomach (pH 2), log [Unionized]/[Ionized] equals:
questions.exp: log [U]/[I] = pKa − pH = 4 − 2 = 2. (Book p6)

questions.q: Continuing the same calculation, [Unionized]/[Ionized] equals:
For an acidic drug of pKa 4 in gastric pH 2, the percentage of drug unionized and ionized is:
questions.exp: A ratio of [U]/[I] = 100 means 99% of the acidic drug is unionized and only 1% ionized — hence it can be absorbed from the stomach. (Book p6)

questions.q: An acidic drug has pKa 4. At a medium pH of 4, the drug will be:
questions.exp: When pH equals pKa, log [U]/[I] = 0, so the ratio is 1:1 — this is the defining situation of pKa (50% ionized, 50% unionized). (Book p6)

questions.q: An acidic drug of pKa 4 is placed in a medium of pH 6. It will be predominantly:
questions.exp: log [U]/[I] = 4 − 6 = −2, so [U]/[I] = 1/100 — the acidic drug is largely ionized in the more alkaline medium and is therefore poorly absorbed. (Book p6)

questions.q: A basic drug of pKa 8 is in the stomach (pH 2). Using log [I]/[U] = pKa − pH, the drug will be:
questions.exp: log [I]/[U] = 8 − 2 = 6, i.e., [I]/[U] = 10⁶ — a basic drug is overwhelmingly ionized in the acidic stomach and is not absorbed there. (Book p6)

questions.q: In the oral drug flowchart, tablet/capsule is first divided into:
questions.exp: The flowchart splits tablet/capsule into IR (Immediate release) and ER (Extended Release); ER then further branches. (Book p6)

questions.q: 'IR' in the oral drug flowchart stands for:
questions.exp: IR = Immediate release, the conventional formulation requiring frequent dosing. (Book p6)

questions.q: 'ER' in the flowchart stands for:
questions.exp: ER = Extended release, which is further divided into SR (sustained release) and CR (controlled release). (Book p6)

questions.q: Under extended release, the two sub-types shown are:
opts: SR: Sustained Release and CR: Controlled Release
IR: Immediate Release and SR: Sustained Release
DR: Delayed Release and ER: Extended Release
CR: Controlled Release and DR: Delayed Release
questions.exp: The flowchart branches ER into 'SR: Sustained Release' and 'CR: Controlled Release'. (Book p6)

questions.q: Which formulation is described as 'AKA zero order CR'?
questions.exp: 'CR: Controlled Release — AKA zero order CR': the controlled release preparation delivers drug at a constant (zero order) rate. (Book p6)

questions.q: The plasma concentration-time curve of an IR preparation with frequent dosing shows:
opts: A shorter peak with prolonged duration
questions.exp: The IR graph shows two successive sharp peaks corresponding to two doses, in contrast to the flat plateau of CR. (Book p6)

questions.q: The mechanism of an IR preparation and its consequence, as given in the flowchart, is:
opts: Frequent dosing leading to decreased compliance
Polymer coating leading to better compliance
Zero order release leading to a plateau
Gastric protection leading to better absorption
questions.exp: Under the IR curve the text reads 'mechanism: Frequent dosing: ↓Compliance'. (Book p6)

questions.q: The example given for an IR preparation dosed TID is:
questions.exp: 'Example: Indomethacin TID' is written under the IR curve; indomethacin IR must be taken three times a day. (Book p6)

questions.q: The SR plasma concentration curve, compared with IR, is described as showing:
opts: Shorter peak and increased duration of action
questions.exp: The SR graph is annotated 'Shorter peak' and '↑Duration of action' — the peak is blunted but drug action lasts longer. (Book p6)

questions.q: Which advantage of SR preparations is stated in the text?
questions.exp: Under SR the text lists 'Better compliance' and 'Polymer coating present', with SR indomethacin as the example. (Book p6)

questions.q: The SR formulation's release is achieved by:
questions.exp: 'Polymer coating present' — SR indomethacin uses a polymer coating to slow drug release. (Book p6)

questions.q: The example given for a sustained release preparation is:
questions.exp: 'SR Indomethacin' is listed under the SR column, just as 'CR Zolpidem' is listed under CR. (Book p6)

questions.q: The CR preparation achieves its profile by:
questions.exp: Under the CR curve the text reads 'Polymer coating of pores' — the drug diffuses out through polymer-coated pores giving zero order release. (Book p6)

questions.q: The example given for a controlled release preparation is:
questions.exp: 'CR Zolpidem' is the example written beside the CR plasma concentration graph. (Book p6)

questions.q: Which formulation's plasma concentration-time curve shows a flat plateau with no peaks?
questions.exp: The CR graph rises to a plateau and stays flat — zero order release maintains a steady plasma concentration. (Book p6)

questions.q: A patient on indomethacin TID three times daily keeps forgetting doses. Which formulation change would best improve compliance?
questions.exp: The book contrasts IR indomethacin TID (frequent dosing, ↓compliance) with SR indomethacin, which has a polymer coating, better compliance, shorter peak and longer duration. (Book p6)

questions.q: Which sequence correctly orders the oral formulation flowchart?
opts: Tablet/Capsule → IR & ER; ER → SR & CR
Tablet/Capsule → SR & CR; SR → IR & ER
Tablet/Capsule → ER & DR; DR → IR & CR
Tablet/Capsule → IR & SR; IR → ER & CR
questions.exp: The flowchart divides tablet/capsule into IR and ER, and divides ER further into SR (sustained release) and CR (controlled release). (Book p6)

questions.q: The two categories of drugs shown bypassing the stomach are:
questions.exp: The page branches 'a. Drugs bypassing the stomach' into 'Delayed release' and 'Enteric coated'. (Book p7)

questions.q: Delayed release preparations are designed to release the drug in the:
opts: Small intestine instead of the stomach
Stomach instead of the small intestine
questions.exp: 'Delayed release: Release of drug in SI instead in stomach.' (Book p7)

questions.q: The example given for a delayed release preparation is:
questions.exp: 'Eg: Sulfasalazine → For ulcerative colitis' — sulfasalazine is formulated for release in the small intestine/colon. (Book p7)

questions.q: Sulfasalazine is given as a delayed release preparation for the treatment of:
questions.exp: The text specifies sulfasalazine for ulcerative colitis, delivered beyond the stomach. (Book p7)

questions.q: The example given for an enteric coated preparation is:
questions.exp: 'Enteric coated: Eg: PPI → Protect from gastric HCl' — the proton pump inhibitor is coated to survive gastric acid. (Book p7)

questions.q: The purpose of enteric coating a PPI is to:
opts: Protect the drug from gastric HCl
Protect the stomach from the drug
questions.exp: The diary states 'Protect from gastric HCl' — the coating shields the acid-labile drug as it passes through the stomach. (Book p7)

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches the preparation with its purpose?
opts: Delayed release → release drug in the small intestine
Enteric coated → release drug in the stomach
Enteric coated → slow release over 24 hours
Delayed release → protect drug from gastric HCl
questions.exp: Delayed release shifts release to the small intestine (e.g., sulfasalazine in ulcerative colitis); enteric coating's purpose is to protect the drug from gastric HCl (e.g., PPI). (Book p7)

questions.q: Bioavailability (F) is defined as the fraction of drug that:
opts: Is absorbed from the small intestine
Escape first pass metabolism in the gut
questions.exp: 'BIOAVAILABILITY (F): Fraction of drug reaches systemic circulation unchanged.' (Book p7)

questions.q: According to the flowchart for factors determining F, the drug reaching the liver after 100% intestinal absorption may undergo:
questions.exp: The flowchart traces: 100% of drug → intestinal absorption → liver → fraction that reaches systemic circulation, while a fraction undergoes first pass metabolism (and a fraction is excreted). (Book p7)

questions.q: Which two situations increase bioavailability (F), as listed in the text?
opts: The drug bypasses the liver, and absorption increases
The drug undergoes first pass metabolism, and absorption decreases
The drug is ionised, and urine is acidified
The drug is water soluble, and Pgp efflux increases
questions.exp: '↑F if → Drug bypasses liver; ↑Absorption occurs' — both raise the fraction reaching the systemic circulation. (Book p7)

questions.q: In the flowchart of factors determining F, the fraction of drug lost on its way to the systemic circulation includes:
opts: Excretion of a fraction and first pass metabolism of a fraction
questions.exp: The flowchart shows that after absorption a fraction is excreted and a fraction undergoes hepatic first pass metabolism, so only the remainder reaches the systemic circulation. (Book p7)

questions.q: The formula for bioavailability given in the box is:
questions.exp: The box reads 'Bioavailability: AUCoral / AUCiv × 100'. (Book p7)

questions.q: In the concentration-time curve, the area under the curve (AUC) represents the:
questions.exp: The text links the AUC to the 'Extent of Drug Absorption' — extent is measured by AUC, whereas rate is measured by Tmax. (Book p7)

questions.q: The only route of administration with 100% bioavailability is:
questions.exp: 'Only route with 100% B.V: I/V' — intravenous administration bypasses absorption and first pass metabolism. (Book p7)

questions.q: On the concentration-time curve, which route gives the immediately maximal plasma concentration at time zero?
questions.exp: The curve is labelled 'IV max' at the highest point at zero time, while the oral curve rises later and shows a smaller AUC. (Book p7)

questions.q: The oral curve in the concentration-time graph lies below the IV curve because of:
opts: First pass metabolism and incomplete absorption
questions.exp: The smaller (oral) AUC compared with IV reflects the fractions lost to excretion and first pass metabolism before the drug reaches the systemic circulation, giving F < 1. (Book p7)

questions.q: As per the table, the bioavailability of the IV route is:
questions.exp: The table lists IV → bioavailability '1', i.e., 100%. (Book p8)

questions.q: As per the table, the bioavailability of the IM/SC route is:
questions.exp: The table lists im/sc → 0.75–1.0, slightly less than the intravenous route but still high. (Book p8)

questions.q: As per the table, the bioavailability of the oral route is:
questions.exp: The table lists oral → 0.05–1.0, the widest range of all routes because first pass metabolism differs from drug to drug. (Book p8)

questions.q: Which route shows the widest range of bioavailability in the table?
questions.exp: Oral spans 0.05–1.0, i.e., from 5% to complete bioavailability, whereas IV is fixed at 1 and im/sc at 0.75–1.0. (Book p8)

questions.q: The note following the route table states that bioavailability does NOT indicate:
questions.exp: 'Note: F does not indicate rate of drug absorption' — F measures the extent (AUC), not the speed, of absorption. (Book p8)

questions.q: Cmax is defined as the:
opts: Maximum plasma concentration achieved by a drug
Time to reach the maximum concentration
questions.exp: 'Cmax: maximum plasma conc achieved by a drug' — it is the peak of the plasma concentration-time curve. (Book p8)

questions.q: Tmax is a marker of the:
questions.exp: 'Tmax: marker of rate of drug absorption' — the sooner the peak occurs, the faster the absorption. (Book p8)

questions.q: Two formulations of the same drug show Tmax of 1 hour and 4 hours respectively. This indicates a difference in:
questions.exp: Tmax is the marker of the rate of drug absorption; extent would instead be compared using AUC. (Book p8)

questions.q: Which parameter reflects the extent, and which reflects the rate, of drug absorption?
questions.exp: The AUC measures the extent of absorption (and hence bioavailability), while Tmax is the marker of the rate of absorption. (Book p8)

questions.q: On the rate-of-absorption graph, the peak of the plasma concentration (PC) curve corresponds to:
questions.exp: The graph marks Cmax at the top of the curve and Tmax on the time axis directly below it. (Book p8)

questions.q: Bioequivalence is defined as two pharmaceutically equivalent compounds with similar:
questions.exp: 'Bioequivalence: Two pharmaceutically equivalent compound with similar rate (Tmax) and extent (AUC) of absorption.' (Book p8)

questions.q: A branded drug is defined in the text as one which is:
opts: A legal copy made after patent expiry
questions.exp: 'Branded drug: One which is invented, patented for 20 years' — during this period no generic copy can be marketed. (Book p8)

questions.q: A generic drug is defined as:
opts: A legal copy of a new drug made after the patent expires
A drug invented and patented for 20 years
A drug with a different active moiety
questions.exp: 'Generic drug: Legal copy of a new drug (Done after patent expires).' (Book p8)

questions.q: The stated benefit of a generic drug is that it is:
questions.exp: 'Benefit of a generic drug: Cheaper' — the generic contains the same drug but costs less. (Book p8)

questions.q: For approval of a generic drug, the required application is:
questions.exp: 'For generic drug approval: ANDA (Abbreviated New Drug Application)' — the abbreviated filing relies on bioequivalence rather than full clinical data. (Book p8)

questions.q: The criteria for approving a generic drug is that it is bioequivalent to the branded drug within:
questions.exp: 'Generic drug = Bioequivalent to Branded drug ± 30%' — the generic must fall within ±30% of the branded product. (Book p8)

questions.q: A generic formulation of a drug has an AUC 20% lower than the branded product, with a similar Tmax. It will be:
opts: Rejected, since any difference is unacceptable
Approved only if Tmax is identical
Rejected, because AUC must be equal
questions.exp: The approval criterion is bioequivalence to the branded drug within ±30%; a 20% difference in AUC with similar rate falls within this limit. (Book p8)

questions.q: Two generic products of the same drug are compared. Bioequivalence between them is judged by similarity of:
questions.exp: Bioequivalence means similar rate (Tmax) and extent (AUC) of absorption; the approval limit against the branded drug is ±30%. (Book p8)

questions.q: Which of the following is TRUE regarding F and Tmax?
opts: F reflects the extent of absorption while Tmax reflects its rate
Both F and Tmax reflect the rate of absorption
Both F and Tmax reflect the extent of absorption
F reflects the rate of absorption while Tmax reflects its extent
questions.exp: F is derived from AUC and denotes the extent of absorption (and does not indicate rate), whereas Tmax is the marker of the rate of drug absorption. (Book p8)

units.title: The Criteria Table: LUNJA for Absorption, WIPE for Excretion
units.guide: One table decides everything: to be absorbed a drug must be lipid soluble, unionised, non-polar with the medium's pH equal to the drug's, and to be excreted it must be water soluble, ionised, polar with the pH of drug and medium unequal. The mnemonics are LUNJA for absorption and WIPE for excretion.

units.title: Acidic in Acid, Basic in Base — and the Duodenum Rule
units.guide: An acidic drug (aspirin) is unionised in the acidic stomach and a basic drug in the basic small intestine. Yet the unionised drug is maximally absorbed in the small intestine — duodenum — simply because of its enormous surface area, which beats the stomach's favourable pH.

units.title: Short Bowel Syndrome: Lose the Gut, Lose the Drug
units.guide: Resection of the small intestine reduces drug absorption, so an oral drug may fail. Management is to increase the dose or change the route — a direct clinical application of surface-area-driven absorption.

units.title: Ion Trapping: Alkalinise for Acid, Acidify for Base
units.guide: Excretion needs the drug ionised, hence the pH of drug and medium must differ. Acidic drug toxicity (aspirin, phenobarbital, methotrexate) is treated by alkalinising urine with bicarbonate; basic drug toxicity (amphetamine) by acidifying urine with ammonium chloride — vitamin C and cranberry juice are other urine acidifiers. Ionised drug is trapped and excreted.

units.title: Henderson-Hasselbalch: Quantifying Ionization
units.guide: For an acidic drug log [U]/[I] = pKa − pH; for a basic drug the ratio is inverted as log [I]/[U] = pKa − pH. pKa is the pH at which half the drug is ionised. An acidic drug of pKa 4 in gastric pH 2 gives a ratio of 100 — 99% unionised and 1% ionised, which is why absorption can occur.

units.title: IR, SR and CR: Three Shapes of a Release Curve
units.guide: A tablet is either immediate release (IR) or extended release (ER), and ER splits into sustained release (SR) and controlled release (CR), the latter also called zero order CR. IR gives repeated sharp peaks with frequent dosing (indomethacin TID) and poor compliance; SR uses a polymer coating for a shorter peak and longer duration; CR coats the pores to give a flat plateau.

units.title: Bypassing the Stomach: Delayed Release & Enteric Coating
units.sec: a. Drugs bypassing the stomach · p7
units.guide: Two tricks avoid the stomach: delayed release, which delivers the drug to the small intestine (sulfasalazine for ulcerative colitis), and enteric coating, which shields an acid-labile drug from gastric HCl (PPIs). One moves the release site, the other protects the drug.

units.title: Bioavailability: Definition, Factors and the AUC Formula
units.guide: Bioavailability is the fraction of drug reaching the systemic circulation unchanged. From 100% intestinal absorption, a fraction is excreted and a fraction undergoes hepatic first pass metabolism, leaving only the rest in circulation. F = AUCoral/AUCiv × 100; AUC is the extent of absorption, and IV is the only route with 100% bioavailability.

units.title: Route by Route: Bioavailability Table
units.guide: IV bioavailability is 1, im/sc 0.75–1.0, and oral the widest range of 0.05–1.0 because first pass metabolism varies by drug. Remember the note: F tells you the extent, never the rate, of absorption.

units.title: Cmax & Tmax: Rate Versus Extent
units.guide: On a plasma concentration-time curve, Cmax is the highest concentration achieved and Tmax is the time at which it occurs. Tmax is the marker of the rate of absorption, while AUC gives the extent — two different questions answered by two different parameters.

units.title: Bioequivalence: Branded, Generic, ANDA & the ±30% Rule
units.guide: Bioequivalence means two pharmaceutically equivalent products with similar rate (Tmax) and extent (AUC) of absorption. The branded drug is invented and patented for 20 years; the generic is a legal copy marketed after patent expiry, cheaper, approved through ANDA provided it is bioequivalent to the branded drug within ±30%.
